docs.title: ET-1 — Revision session (27 Aug 2026)
docs.text:
~15 min read · T1-2026 paper walkthrough · Solved paper · Week 2 notes

This session walked through the January 2026 AN paper question by question. Nearly every concept below has a solved PYQ with full reasoning — this page records what the professor said about it, in enough detail that you're hearing him explain it.

docs.title: The exam format (announced this session)
docs.text:
Straight from the professor

  • The paper will have MCQs, MSQs, and numerical problems — plus subjective questions, newly introduced. "A staple at the degree level to test depth."
  • Practice PYQs on the portal — but "don't take a very old paper, which might not be very relevant." The recent-era papers are the guide.
  • If you see a 500 error in a scenario, the debugging focus is the backend code and database layers — not the frontend.

A student asked him to explain the concept behind each question, not just the answer. He agreed — and spent the session doing exactly that. The message: the exam tests whether you understand why a system behaves the way it does, not whether you've memorized the answer.

docs.title: CORS — the security rationale, not just the definition
docs.text:
The scenario he walked through: a frontend application running on localhost:3000 tries to fetch data from a backend API on localhost:8000. The browser throws a CORS error.

First, what "origin" means: an origin is scheme + domain + port. Even though both applications are on the same machine (localhost), the different port numbers make them different origins. The browser treats them as strangers.

His reasoning for why the policy exists — worth remembering word-for-word:

Modern web applications rely on heavily nested third-party JavaScript libraries. If a library is compromised, it could execute unauthorized requests to an external server and exfiltrate sensitive client data. The Same-Origin Policy acts as a guardrail to stop this exfiltration.

Picture the attack: you're logged into your bank in one tab (your browser holds your session). You open evil.com in another tab. Evil.com's JavaScript tries fetch("https://bank.com/api/me") — the browser blocks the read, because bank.com never said evil.com could listen. Without the policy, a single compromised npm package on any website could silently read your data from every other site you're logged into.

The fix: the destination server must explicitly configure its headers to allow the calling origin. In FastAPI, that's the CORS middleware with allow_origins=["http://localhost:3000"].

He also clarified what CORS is not: it's not a server error. curl, Postman, and Python scripts are never blocked by CORS — only browser JavaScript is. Your API may even be working perfectly when the browser shows a CORS error; it's the browser's read that's refused.

Asked in 6 places: T1-AN Q13 — the fix · T1-AN Q18 — the error side · T1-FN Q2 — the reason · T1-FN Q18 — the local HTML block · Week 2 — CORS section · GA2

docs.title: GitHub Pages — static only, and why the form fails
docs.text:
The scenario: a student deploys a portfolio website to GitHub Pages and tries to add a Python FastAPI backend to handle form submissions directly on the platform.

His explanation: GitHub Pages is exclusively designed to serve static files — HTML, CSS, images, and client-side JavaScript assets. There is no backend runtime execution environment, no database storage, no Python process. The form submission simply has nothing to receive it — it's like mailing a letter to an address that has no mailbox.

The correct architecture: static frontend on Pages, backend on a real runtime (a Cloud Function, a container, a server). This exact scenario became a short-answer question in the FN shift (T1-FN Q3).

Asked in: T1-FN Q3 — the form submission failure · Week 2 — deployment platforms

docs.title: JSON parsing — the single-quote crash (demonstrated live)
docs.text:
He showed this code on screen:

import json

# This throws json.decoder.JSONDecodeError because of single quotes
try:
    json.loads("{'score': 10}")
except json.decoder.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

# Correct version using double quotes inside the string
valid_json = json.loads('{"score": 10}')
print(valid_json['score'])  # Output: 10

The rule: standard JSON requires double quotes for keys and string values. Python dictionary syntax ({'score': 10}) uses single quotes and is not JSON. The parser is strict — even if a string looks like a valid Python dict, json.loads rejects it if it breaks the double-quote specification.

This pairs with the response.text vs response.json() distinction he also covered: .text gives you the raw string, .json() parses it into a dictionary you can index. After .json() you can write data["score"]; after .text you can't.

Asked in: T1-AN Q7 — .text vs .json() · T1-FN Q4 — response.json() · T1-FN Q20 — the malformed JSON crash

docs.title: Docker — environment parity + the missing install
docs.text:
Scenario 1 (parity): you build a Docker image locally on Linux and push it to Docker Hub. Your colleague pulls it on Windows. The code runs Ubuntu Linux inside the container. What happens?

His explanation: Docker's core design is to package and configure the entire runtime environment starting from the operating system level. Because the OS and dependencies are completely encapsulated inside the image, it runs successfully on Windows (or any platform) with exact parity. The "works on my machine" problem dies here — every machine running the container is the same machine.

Scenario 2 (the crash): a Python web app container crashes immediately with "cannot find the requests library." What's missing?

His explanation: Docker containers are completely isolated. You must explicitly write commands in the Dockerfile to install every single dependency required by your script. The crash occurs because the package installation step was omitted:

# The missing line:
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

He paired these two ideas deliberately: parity works because isolation is total. The same wall that keeps your laptop's environment out is what makes the container identical everywhere.

Asked in: T1-FN Q5 — parity · T1-FN Q11 — the missing install · T3-FN Q30 — the install line · Week 2 — Docker section

docs.title: HTTPS — the Caesar cipher explanation
docs.text:
A student (Disha Rani) asked what "encrypts data" actually means. His answer, in full:

Encryption is a cybersecurity concept where you run plaintext data through a mathematical algorithm to scramble it into randomized text that nobody can understand during transmission. He explained it with the Caesar cipher (a Roman-era textbook example):

  • Set the shift key to n = 2
  • Every letter shifts forward by 2: 'a' → 'c', 'h' → 'j', 'e' → 'g'
  • Instead of transmitting "Hello World" in cleartext, the sender transmits the shifted ciphertext
  • The receiver applies the reverse shift (subtract 2) to recover the plaintext

His practical warning: the Caesar cipher is absolutely not used in modern web protocols — but it's the perfect mental model for what encryption does. HTTPS does the same thing (scramble in transit, unscramble at the ends) with industrial-strength mathematics.

Why it matters for API tokens: if you send a token over plain HTTP, it travels in cleartext — anyone intercepting the network traffic reads it. HTTPS encrypts the payload so only the sender and receiver can decode it.

Asked in: T1-FN Q6 — why HTTPS for tokens · Week 2 — deployment

docs.title: asyncio.gather — the bottleneck arithmetic
docs.text:
The scenario: you trigger 5 network requests in parallel using asyncio.gather. Four complete in exactly 1 second; one takes 10 seconds.

His explanation, step by step:

  1. asyncio.gather runs all provided functions concurrently — all 5 launch simultaneously
  2. Four finish after 1 second, but gather cannot yield the final combined response until every registered task completes
  3. It must block and wait for the slowest task
  4. Total execution time: 10 seconds

The key insight: concurrency removes the sum (which would be 14 seconds sequentially: 4×1 + 10), not the max. Parallelism does not fix a single slow dependency — the hanger holds everything hostage. In the scenario version (T1-AN Q21), one node hangs for 60 seconds and the entire server process halts — which is why production code wraps each call in asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=...).

Asked in: T1-AN Q21 — the hanging server · T1-FN Q7 — the timing question · Week 5 — async section

docs.title: Secret keys — the .env workflow and the .gitignore oversight
docs.text:
His exact workflow:

  1. Never hardcode or type private API/secret keys directly into Python files
  2. Store them in a local .env file
  3. Immediately add .env to .gitignore — the oversight he named specifically: "developers often remember to use .env files but forget to list them in .gitignore"
  4. Load in code with os.getenv("API_KEY")

The risk, in his words: if you forget the .gitignore and push to GitHub, your .env file with secret keys goes to the public web. Rogue actors can scrape your repository, copy your keys, and impersonate you — resulting in a security disaster: data breaches, financial loss.

The key point about git history: once a secret is pushed, it's in the history forever. Deleting the file in a later commit doesn't remove it from earlier commits — anyone who clones the repo has the full history including the secret. This is why the workflow must be right from the first commit.

Asked in 5+ places: T1-AN Q5 — the .gitignore MSQ · T1-FN Q8 — why .env exists · T3-AN Q24 — where the key lives · T3-FN Q6 — environment variables · Week 2 — secrets section

docs.title: Serverless memory limits — the 2GB file story
docs.text:
The scenario: a script loads a 2GB file into memory. It works perfectly on your laptop but repeatedly crashes with "Out of Memory" on a free-tier Cloud Function.

His explanation: serverless Cloud Functions run in lightweight virtual environments that enforce very strict RAM limits — typically 128–512 MB on free tiers. Trying to read a massive file in one go exceeds the allocation, and the operating system immediately terminates the process.

The numbers to remember: your laptop has 8–32 GB of RAM; a free-tier function has 128–512 MB. Local success proves nothing about a constrained environment.

The fix: optimize data loading — streaming, chunking, reading only what you need — instead of loading everything into memory at once. Or move the job to a container where you control the resources.

This is the RAM twin of the timeout story (T1-AN Q17): serverless gives you strict memory and strict time. Together they're the platform's fundamental trade-off — you get zero-ops deployment, but you live within hard ceilings.

Asked in: T1-FN Q10 — the RAM limit · T1-AN Q17 — the time twin · Week 2 — serverless section

docs.title: Prompt injection filters — case variation defeats matching
docs.text:
The scenario: an application filters out the word "ignore" to prevent prompt injections. A user types "IGNORE" in capital letters and successfully bypasses the filter.

His explanation: relying on exact string-matching filters is incredibly weak. Users can bypass them with basic variations in casing, spelling, or formatting:

  • "ignore" → blocked
  • "IGNORE" → passes (different case)
  • "I-g-n-o-r-e" → passes (hyphenated)
  • "1gn0re" → passes (leetspeak)

The robust solution he gave: convert the incoming user text to lowercase before evaluation, then use Regular Expressions (Regex) to flag pattern matches rather than checking exact words. The regex catches ignore, IGNORE, Ign0re and variants — because it matches the pattern, not the string.

He connected this to the deeper defense in the next topic: role separation (system vs user prompts) is the structural protection; filtering is one layer on top.

Asked in: T1-FN Q12 — why the bypass works · T1-FN Q23 — the robust filter · Week 7 — LLM security

docs.title: Caching — the Twitter slow-network example
docs.text:
A student (Manoj Kumar Khatri) said: "I can't understand caching." His answer, in full:

The example: load Twitter on a slow internet connection. You'll notice the sidebar templates, static images, and structural UI elements render instantly — no lag — even though the actual tweets take a long time to load. This is because Twitter caches those static assets directly inside your local browser's storage. Your browser loads them from disk instead of wasting bandwidth fetching them over the slow network.

The header: Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 does two things:

  • public authorizes intermediate proxies and CDNs to serve cached copies directly
  • max-age=3600 means the copy is fresh for 3600 seconds (1 hour)

The benefit: subsequent identical requests never reach your origin backend server — saving massive amounts of network bandwidth and compute.

The cache-buster: what if you update your profile picture but the browser cached the old one for 2 hours? The client's JavaScript can append a random query parameter (?t=1 or ?time=123) to the URL. Because the URL changed, it mutates the cache key — the browser/CDN sees it as a completely new request and must fetch fresh from the server.

Asked in 8+ places: T1-AN Q19 — what max-age does · T1-AN Q22 — the cache-buster · T1-FN Q13 + Q19 + Q21 · T3-FN Q9 — the dashboard TTL · Week 2 — caching section

docs.title: LLM prompts — system vs user hierarchy
docs.text:
His explanation: developers split inputs into two roles:

  • System prompt (or developer prompt): declares core operational rules — "you are a strict SQL compiler assistant," "always respond in JSON," safety constraints
  • User prompt: carries the transient, user-supplied input — the actual question

Large Language Models are mathematically tuned to assign significantly higher attention weights to system prompts. This hierarchy ensures the model adheres to its core operational rules and safety constraints even if a user tries to override them in their prompt. Separating the inputs prevents users from easily tricking the model — the LLM obeys system instructions much more diligently than user instructions.

This is the structural defense behind the injection-filter question above: role separation is the wall; filtering is a screen door on top of it.

Asked in: T1-AN Q23 — defending the LLM · T1-FN Q15 — why the separation works · Week 3 — prompt engineering

docs.title: Database race conditions — the simultaneous signup
docs.text:
The scenario: two users attempt to sign up with the exact same username at the same millisecond. Your server checks if the username exists, then adds it if available — without any locking.

His explanation, step by step:

  1. Both requests arrive simultaneously
  2. The server checks availability for both at the same time — before either has committed a write
  3. Both checks return "available" (neither write has happened yet)
  4. Both processes attempt to write to the database
  5. Result: duplicate user records, or a database integrity exception

This is a check-then-act race — the gap between reading a state and acting on it is where the second process sneaks in. The fix: make check-and-write atomic — a database lock, a unique constraint (the database itself rejects the second insert), or a transaction with proper isolation.

Nothing else in the stack rescues you for free — not Python, not the network, not the database on its default settings.

Asked in: T1-FN Q16 — the race condition

docs.title: ML data leakage — memorization vs generalization
docs.text:
The scenario: a team discovers 200 test reviews accidentally appeared in their training data. After removing duplicates and retraining, accuracy drops from 94% to 76%.

His explanation: this is classic data leakage. When a model is exposed to test-set data during its training phase, it memorizes the correct answers for those specific examples rather than learning the generalized patterns. The 94% was the model reciting answers it had already seen — not real understanding.

Once the leaked records are removed, the model can no longer rely on memory. The 76% is the true accuracy — what the model actually learned about patterns it has never seen before.

The signature the exam rewards: suspiciously high test accuracy + shared rows between train and test = leakage until proven otherwise. The T1-AN version (Q16) adds how leakage happens in practice: shuffling a chronological dataset (temporal leakage) and computing rolling statistics before the train/test split (feature leakage).

Asked in: T1-AN Q16 — the fraud model · T1-FN Q17 — the 94% to 76% drop

docs.title: API gateway + redundancy — the 80-microservice story
docs.text:
The scenario: a massive application serves 50 million users across 200 countries, with 80 different backend microservices — user profiles, recommendations, video encoding, billing, analytics. Managing 80 endpoints created chaos: hardcoded URLs broke during migrations, each service implemented its own authentication inconsistently.

His explanation:

The problem with hardcoded URLs: mobile developers embedded 80 different API URLs directly in the client code. When servers migrated, every URL broke — and updating a mobile app to fix URLs takes days (app store review).

What an API gateway is: a single, unified entry point. It uses centralized routing rules and path-matching logic to accept client requests and forward them to the correct backend service. It also centralizes authentication — users authenticate once at the gateway using OAuth tokens, instead of 80 services each implementing their own auth.

The single point of failure: one gateway instance means one failure away from total outage. During a traffic spike, the gateway crashes and the entire platform goes down — even though all 80 backend services are running fine. The fix: deploy multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer — if one dies, others handle the traffic.

Debugging with a gateway: a 500 error could now originate from the gateway's routing logic, the authentication middleware, the backend service, or the network between layers — you must check every layer the request crossed.

Asked in: T1-FN Q26 — who routes · T1-FN Q27 — surviving the crash · T1-FN Q28 — debugging the 500

docs.title: Student doubts worth recording
docs.text: Student asked The professor's answer What does "encrypts data" mean? (Disha Rani) Plaintext → algorithm → randomized ciphertext. Explained via Caesar cipher (shift 2): 'a'→'c', 'h'→'j'. The receiver unshifts to decrypt. I can't understand caching. (Manoj Kumar Khatri) Twitter on slow network: UI renders from local cache, tweets lag. max-age=3600 authorizes CDNs to serve copies. Cache-buster: ?t=1 changes the cache key. What happens with concurrent signups? (Manoj Kumar Khatri) Without database locks, both checks pass simultaneously, both write — the race condition. Fixed by explicit locking or unique constraints. Please explain the concept behind each question. (Manoj Kumar Khatri) He agreed — and explained the underlying mechanics behind every practice question for the rest of the session.

docs.title: ET-2 — Revision session (28 Aug 2026)
docs.text:
~15 min read · T3-2025 FN paper walkthrough · Solved paper · The LLM-grading reveal

This session walked through the September 2025 FN paper. It also carried the new exam format announcement and the syllabus exclusion. Links go to the solved paper.

docs.title: The new exam format (the biggest reveal)
docs.text:
Straight from the professor — memorize this

  • Two question types: standard MCQs matching previous papers, plus new subjective scenario-based questions testing critical thinking rather than rote definitions or technical trivia.
  • Subjective questions are graded by LLMs (AI-graded, not humans). Success depends on organizing, structuring, and justifying your answers clearly enough to "convince the LM."
  • Example subjective scenario: you're talking to a client — "What are the three most important follow-up questions you would ask based on these requirements?" — testing whether you think about capabilities, constraints, and business context before building.
  • For the LLM grader: use bullet points and clear headers. It grades on logical markers and "thinking" keywords: constraints, assumptions, scalability.
  • On answer length: "logic over length" — a reasoned solution that demonstrates critical thinking, not a high word count.

Why this matters more than any single topic: the subjective section is new (first appeared in Jan 2026) and growing. Students who can't write for an LLM grader lose marks that no amount of MCQ knowledge recovers. Our full method with worked examples: Writing answers an LLM grades well.

Syllabus exclusion

OpenRefine is NOT on this term's syllabus. If you encounter OpenRefine questions in older papers (text clustering, name standardization), skip them immediately. You will not be asked.

docs.title: Parquet — the "odd one out"
docs.text:
JSON, XML, and CSV are all text-based formats — human-readable, "flat," and carrying significant overhead when storing large numeric arrays (every number becomes a string of characters, and the parser must convert back).

Parquet uses a columnar approach — values of each column live together in a binary format, which makes it "the odd one out" and the most efficient choice for heavy numerical data.

Why columnar wins for analytics: when you query two columns of a twenty-column table, a row-based format (CSV) forces you to scan every row to extract those two values. A columnar format lets you read only the two columns you need — a fraction of the bytes, a fraction of the network transfer for remote files.

The exam pattern he named: when a question groups XML, JSON, and CSV together and asks about efficiency, the columnar outlier (Parquet) is almost certainly the correct answer.

Asked in: T3-FN Q2 — Parquet for arrays · T1-AN Q4 — Parquet vs CSV speed

docs.title: Git lifecycle — the "safety goggles" before welding
docs.text:
He walked through the full inspection family, then gave it a metaphor worth keeping:

git status and git diff are the safety goggles you must wear before performing the welding of a commit or push. They prevent the accidental introduction of breaking changes into the shared codebase.

Command What it shows When to use it git status Which files changed, staged, or untracked Before every commit git diff What lines changed (working directory vs last commit) Before every commit git log Commit history — authors, timestamps, messages Finding when something broke git show One specific commit's changes in detail Investigating a single change

The trap he didn't mention but the exam tests: git diff after git add shows nothing — by default it compares the working directory to the staging area, not the last commit. git diff --staged shows what's actually about to be committed.

Asked in: T3-FN Q3 — git diff · T3-FN Q23–27 — the full git workflow scenario · Week 1 — git section

docs.title: HTTP status codes — the full taxonomy
docs.text:
He taught the complete family with a distinction students consistently confuse:

Code Meaning His example 401 Unauthorized Authentication required or failed — who are you? Viewing private Instagram content without an account 403 Forbidden Authenticated but lacking permission — I know you, but you can't do this Logged in, but viewing someone else's private content 404 Not Found The resource doesn't exist — 429 Too Many Requests Rate limit exceeded Often triggered/handled by the API library itself 500 Internal Server Error Generic server-side failure — the client request was valid Check backend code and database

The 401 vs 403 distinction is the one to nail: identity vs permission. One is a locked door with no key; the other is a key that doesn't fit this lock.

His note on 429: in many modern implementations, this code is handled by the API library itself — it retries with exponential backoff without you writing retry logic. But you should still know what the code means.

On 500: the generic catch-all for server-side failures where the client did nothing wrong. The debugging focus: backend code execution and the database layer — not the frontend.

Asked in: T3-AN Q4 — the 401 · T3-FN Q4 — the 429 · T1-FN Q28 — debugging the 500 · T3-AN Q27 — the 401 in a scenario

docs.title: API validation — fail fast with schemas
docs.text:
His framing: external APIs (like Gemini or weather services) are unpredictable. Data may be missing, or the server may time out. Your architecture must survive this.

The strategy — fail fast:

  • Audit data types and value ranges immediately upon receipt — at the boundary, before anything downstream
  • Reject with clear error messages that a human can act on (which field, what's wrong)
  • Explicit fallback strategies — so one API failure doesn't crash the entire downstream pipeline

Why "let downstream handle it" fails: bad data that flows past the boundary corrupts something far from its cause — the most expensive kind of bug to diagnose. The error appears in a dashboard three steps later, and nobody remembers which API call introduced the bad row.

Asked in: T3-FN Q7 — validation strategy · T3-AN Q17 — schema validation · T1-FN Q14 — Pydantic coercion

docs.title: ETL — lookback windows, not full reprocessing
docs.text:
The problem: late-arriving or updated data that belongs to a previous processing cycle. Orders placed two days ago get updated today — but your pipeline already processed "two days ago" and won't look back.

The wrong fix: reprocess all historical data daily. He called this "cost-extensive" — wasted compute credits, excessive processing time, potential database lockups. In production, this is considered a failure of design.

The right pattern:

  1. Lookback window — process only the last N days (typically 3), capturing late arrivals without touching history
  2. Deduplication — key on (order_id, update_timestamp) so re-seeing a row is harmless: the newest version wins, duplicates collapse

The exam connection: this exact pattern appears as both an MCQ (T3-FN Q8) and as the TDS tip in a short-answer question: "use terms like 'Lookback Window' and 'Deduplication'" — the LLM grader rewards the professional vocabulary.

Asked in: T3-FN Q8 — the lookback pattern · T3-AN Q11 — idempotent ETL · GA2 (api-idempotency-pagination-server)

docs.title: Dashboard caching — TTL arithmetic
docs.text:
The setup: a dashboard queries a large dataset that updates hourly but is viewed (queried) every few seconds by users.

His arithmetic: without caching, the database gets hit ~3600 times per hour (once per few seconds). With a 5-minute TTL, the database is hit once every 5 minutes — regardless of how many users view the dashboard. The cache absorbs the read load; the TTL bounds the freshness loss.

The trade-off TTL embodies: data freshness vs database conservation. A 1-minute TTL is fresher but hits the database more; a 1-hour TTL is very conservative but serves stale data. The right number matches your data's update frequency and your users' tolerance.

Asked in: T3-FN Q9 — the dashboard TTL · T1-AN Q19 — what max-age does · Week 2 — caching

docs.title: Timezones — the assumption that corrupts silently
docs.text:
His warning: assuming missing timestamps are UTC is "a common and dangerous pitfall that leads to silent data corruption."

What "silent" means here: no error, no warning — the data just shifts by hours. An order that was placed at 2 PM local time gets recorded as 2 PM UTC, which is actually 7:30 PM IST. Every join against another timezone-aware dataset is now off by 5.5 hours. Orders appear before they were placed.

The professional approach, in three steps:

  1. Infer the timezone from metadata or geographic location (where the data came from)
  2. Document the assumption — write down what you inferred and why
  3. Flag inferred values — mark the rows so auditors and downstream users know what's certain vs guessed

The contrast with the naive approach: assume-and-forget is the bug; assume-and-document is engineering.

Asked in: T3-FN Q10 — the timezone approach

docs.title: Docker — the EXPOSE misconception and the build order
docs.text:
The distinction a student asked about:

EXPOSE serves as documentation — a "label" telling other containers which port the app listens on. It is not a "bridge" to the host. Only the -p flag at runtime actually maps the port to the external world.

On seeing Dockerfiles in the exam: a student asked if they'd see a physical Dockerfile. His answer: the file itself may not always be displayed, but you're expected to understand the logic of the build process — the order of operations, what each instruction does, and why the sequence matters.

The sequence that matters most (the layer-caching question from T1-AN Q24):

FROM python:3.12
COPY requirements.txt .      # ← dependency list FIRST
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt   # ← install (stays cached)
COPY . .                     # ← code LAST

Reverse the COPY order and every code edit invalidates the install layer — dependencies re-download on every build.

Asked in: T3-FN Q31 — what EXPOSE does · T3-FN Q30 — the install line · T1-AN Q28 — EXPOSE vs -p · T1-AN Q24 — layer caching SA

docs.title: The restaurant reviews case study (pandas)
docs.text:
He walked through the full scenario — the one that appears as five exam questions in T3-FN Q18–22:

The setup: a food delivery platform with review data in CSV (ratings, text comments, timestamps). They want trending cuisines and satisfaction patterns.

Step 1 — Missing review text:

df.dropna(subset=['review_text'])

His reasoning: for text analysis, rows with no text are pure noise. Keeping nulls "provides zero value for text analysis and skews your statistical averages." But note the scope: you drop these rows for the text analysis — their ratings still count elsewhere. Cleaning is per-question, not global.

Step 2 — Common words in negative reviews:

Filter first (rating < 3.0), then extract and count words from the filtered review_text. Two independent operations chained — don't count all words then filter.

Step 3 — Average rating by cuisine:

df.groupby('cuisine')['rating'].mean()

He noted the column names are case-sensitive — 'Cuisine' and 'cuisine' are different columns.

Step 4 — Sharing with a non-technical manager:

CSV — because it opens in Excel with zero friction. His reasoning: "portability and ease of use." A pickle file requires Python, JSON requires a programmer, a database requires a database.

Asked in: T3-FN Q18 — dropna · T3-FN Q19 — filter then count · T3-FN Q20 — CSV for stakeholders · T3-FN Q21 — pandas · T3-FN Q22 — groupby

docs.title: Rapid-fire best practices
docs.text:
His list, verbatim — each one a potential MCQ or a bullet in a subjective answer:

  • Versioned pipelines: always version transformation logic — it changes more frequently than the data schema
  • Currency storage: store the original amount plus the specific exchange rate used, to enable future audits
  • Recommendation auditing: use systematic segment analysis to fix poorly performing recommendations — not "retrain with more data and hope"
  • Third-party assessment: evaluate security vulnerabilities in external libraries before performing updates — not after
  • Docker reproducibility: use containers and pinned dependencies — "it works on my machine" must translate to the server
  • PII minimization: retain only the fields necessary for the specific utility — balance analysis with privacy

Asked in: T3-FN Q11 — versioning transforms · T3-FN Q12 — currency storage · T3-FN Q13 — segment analysis · T3-FN Q14 — vulnerable dependencies · T3-FN Q15 — reproducibility · T3-FN Q17 — PII minimization

docs.title: Exam-engineering tips (his own framing)
docs.text:
Two patterns he named explicitly

  • The 'Odd One Out' technique: in serialization questions, if you see XML, JSON and CSV grouped together, recognize they're all text-based. Parquet, the columnar outlier, is almost certainly the correct answer for efficiency queries.
  • The 'Longest Option' pattern: in engineering exams, the most detailed answer — the one defining constraints, documenting assumptions, addressing edge cases — is frequently correct because it mirrors professional best practices.

His MCQ prep advice

The MCQ section is designed to be accessible. Reviewing previous year questions is the single most effective use of your study time. The options themselves are designed to guide you — systematic elimination works. By reviewing the choices methodically, you can often eliminate two clearly wrong options and choose between the remaining two on principle.

A reasoned solution demonstrating critical thinking to the LLM grader, not word count. What is "TDL"? A slip of the tongue during the session. The correct term is TTL (Time-To-Live). TDL is not a standard term in this curriculum. Will we see a Dockerfile in the exam? The file itself may not always be displayed, but you're expected to understand the logic of the build process (e.g., the order of operations). What does EXPOSE do? docs.title: ET-3 — Final revision session (3 Sept 2026)
docs.text:
~12 min read · no paper this time — the professor talked about the exam itself · the 50% subjective split · reasoning over syntax

The last revision session before the ET, and the most important one: no paper walkthrough this time. The professor explained what the end-term will actually look like this term — and it's a bigger change than the earlier sessions suggested.

docs.title: The exam this term — what he said
docs.text:
The format, straight from the professor

  • About half the paper is subjective questions. The other half stays objective (MCQ/MSQ-style). Roughly 20 marks each on the 40-mark paper.
  • The question structure will be new. He said the formats test structural thinking in ways "probably something you have never seen in the diploma level so far." Concepts you know, asked in new shapes.
  • One confirmed question format: you get a software problem (say, a buggy script) and must write the prompt you'd give a coding agent (like Codex) to solve it. Your prompt-writing is the answer.
  • No live evaluation. Unlike GAs, there's no green-tick loop — submissions are collected first (like an ROE) and evaluated afterward. Check your own logic before submitting.
  • Syntax is not the metric. "We are least concerned about syntax." No writing exact YAML, no exact Dockerfile strings. What's graded: approach, reasoning, critical thinking.
  • No pen-and-paper calculations — it's a reasoning exam.

How to read this: the professor kept repeating one theme — the "why" behind the "how." Commands and syntax are tools; the exam measures whether you can justify and design. That's good news: it rewards understanding the concepts this site already teaches, and it makes rote memorization worthless.

PYQs — how to use them

Asked whether PYQs still help (the syllabus has changed), he said: use them to predict the core concepts, not the exact questions. And don't take a deep dive into very old papers — the most recent three papers are enough. We hold exactly those four sessions' worth; see the solved papers.

docs.title: Relative grading — how the final grade works
docs.text:
The professor explained the mechanics of the bell curve:

  • Marks are normalized across the cohort — your grade depends on how you perform relative to everyone else, not just your raw score.
  • Statistically, about half the cohort falls below the median, whatever the paper's difficulty.
  • Projects are the exception: the team plans to make the project grader public (criteria and test cases visible) — project grading stays absolute, not relative.

What this means for you: on a hard paper, everyone's score drops — the curve restores the balance. Don't panic if the paper feels tough; it feels tough for everyone, and only your relative position matters.

Bonus marks — 99% not happening

A student asked if bonus marks are final. The team found no major unresolvable issues in the assessments, so: "99% we won't be having bonus." For GA5's buggy final question, the fix was a deadline extension + a more permissive grader, not flat compensation. Plan your score calculations without bonus.

docs.title: Case study: the sentiment API (his example of a subjective question)
docs.text:
This is the sample subjective scenario he walked through — a student's FastAPI sentiment analysis endpoint from a previous term:

The symptoms:

  • Invalid inputs cause silent downstream failures — no clear errors
  • An empty text parameter still returns "positive" — the service "works" while doing nothing

The real flaw he pointed at: the endpoint function stores a hardcoded placeholder in a variable and returns it directly. It never reads the request body, never runs any model. He called this "functionally dead" — and the point of the question is not to hunt for syntax typos, but to identify this semantic flaw.

What a strong answer fixes (under 200 words):

  1. Real inference — replace the hardcoded return with an actual model call
  2. Input validation — Pydantic schema + type hints at the boundary; reject empty strings with a clear 400
  3. Exception handling — catch malformed JSON and inference timeouts instead of failing silently

docs.title: GET vs POST — the follow-up he guaranteed
docs.text:
For an ML inference endpoint, GET is a design flaw:

GET POST Where the text goes URL query params request body Who sees it browser history, proxy logs, network trails nobody in transit logs Long documents fails — strict URL length limits fine Auth headers awkward clean, standard

The one-line answer to remember: POST encapsulates the payload safely in the body, has no length limit, and carries authentication headers — GET exposes input in logs and breaks on long text.

Related: Web & APIs — status codes · T1-FN Q28 — debugging the 500 · practice: spot-the-bug questions

docs.title: Shell config — source and the current session
docs.text:
Environment variables live in ~/.bashrc (the config file your shell reads at startup). Add one:

export API_KEY="dev_99x"   # appended to ~/.bashrc

The trap: a new line in .bashrc does nothing to your already-open terminal. The file is only read at shell startup.

The fix — run the file inside your current session:

source ~/.bashrc   # or the shorthand:  . ~/.bashrc

source executes every line of the file in your live shell, so new variables, aliases, and functions register immediately — no restart.

Related: Week notes — tools & fundamentals · cheat sheet

docs.title: grep -r — don't forget the dot
docs.text:
The correct command to search recursively for "input" from where you stand:

grep -r "input" .
  • -r — recursive: search every file, then dive into every subdirectory
  • . — the search origin: the current directory

The trap he named: omit the dot and grep waits on stdin — the terminal looks hung, but it's actually waiting for you to pipe data in. Nothing is broken; nothing was searched.

docs.title: Shebang — when #! matters and when it doesn't
docs.text:
The shebang (#!/bin/bash) is a kernel directive read only when you run a script directly as an executable (./script.sh). The OS reads the interpreter path, launches it, and pipes your file into it.

The override rule (his doubt-session answer): if you invoke the interpreter explicitly — python3 script.sh — the shebang is completely ignored. The command line wins. That's why a .sh file with a bash shebang can still execute under python3 (and produce bash syntax errors).

Do you need to write shebangs in the exam? No absolute requirement — shebangs only enable self-executability.

docs.title: The os module — Python's bridge to the system
docs.text:
Function Purpose os.environ / os.environ.get("KEY") read (and write) environment variables — .get() returns None instead of raising KeyError os.chmod() change file permissions os.cpu_count() logical CPUs — not physical chips os.chroot() change the active root directory

The distinction he drilled: os.cpu_count() counts logical threads (with hyper-threading, typically 2× the physical cores) — not silicon chips.

Reading an API key safely:

import os
api_key = os.environ.get("Apk")   # None if missing, no crash

His study tip: learn any module from the terminal — import os, then help(os) — the built-in docs, no browser needed.

docs.title: VS Code — Command Palette vs file search
docs.text:
Shortcut What it does Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac) Command Palette — runs actions (e.g. "Reload Window") Ctrl+P quick-open — searches file names

The Palette is one searchable bar for everything the editor can do — a pattern borrowed from Emacs. Press Ctrl+P and delete the > to switch from commands to filenames.

docs.title: The traps from this session
docs.text:
• 🔴 GET for ML inference — exposes input in logs, breaks on long text. The answer is always POST.
  • 🔴 Single quotes in JSON — json.loads("{'score': 10}") fails: standard JSON requires double quotes.
  • 🔴 .bashrc without sourcing — changes don't apply to the open terminal. source it.
  • 🔴 grep -r without the dot — looks hung, actually waiting on stdin.
  • 🔴 os.cpu_count() = physical chips — no: logical threads.
  • 🔴 "Write this in Python" as a whole prompt — too vague; a good agent prompt carries role, context, task, and constraints.

docs.title: What this session changes about your prep
docs.text:
1. Half your marks come from writing. The LLM-grading guide is now the highest-value page on this site — read it, then practice with the mocks and the short-answer bank.
  2. Study concepts, not answers. PYQs tell you which concepts get asked — the question shapes will be new. Our topic pages and short notes exist exactly for this.
  3. Practice writing agent prompts. It's a confirmed question format: given a problem, write the prompt for Codex — with role, context, task, and constraints. The LLM & prompting notes cover the structure.
  4. Recent papers only. The last three papers are enough — exactly the ones solved on this site.

docs.title: Short notes — the last-minute layer
docs.text:
~40 minutes total · every examinable concept in 60-second sheets · cheat sheet for the final hour

One concept per sheet: what it is, the trap, and a practice question that tests it. Built for the last two days before the exam — skim the category you're weakest in, or read all six in one sitting.

How to use these

  • 2 days out: read all six categories (~40 min), ticking off concepts you know cold
  • 1 day out: re-read only the ones you ticked as shaky
  • Last hour: the cheat sheet — every must-remember on one page

docs.title: The paper
docs.text:
• 80 marks · 90 minutes · Section 1: 30 MCQ/MSQ, 39 marks (official topics 1–5) · Section 2: 9 written, 41 marks (topic 6) · no negative marking — answer everything

The six official topics (memorize the list): 1. Observability & Monitoring · 2. Data Pipeline Integrity · 3. CI/CD & Release Security · 4. Reliable AI/LLM Systems · 5. Web/API/Infra Fundamentals · 6. Applied AI Judgment - MCQ + MSQ + numerical + short answers (LLM-graded) - Marks ramp: 1-mark warm-ups → 2-mark reasoning → 3-mark diagnosis → scenario blocks → SA - The big marks are at the END — move briskly through Part 1

docs.title: Short answers (the new section)
docs.text: Conclusion first → bold-reason bullets → one assumption/trade-off last. Keywords the LLM grader wants: constraints, assumptions, scalability. Logic over length — 120–170 words.

docs.title: The professor's strategy hints
docs.text:
• Options are designed to guide you — eliminate the nonsense, the answer is what's left
  • "Odd one out" (Parquet among text formats) → the outlier is the answer
  • Longest, most detailed option in design questions → frequently correct

docs.title: 🟢 Must-remember — the green boxes
docs.text: Topic The one thing CORS Origin = scheme+host+port. Only the backend can fix it (add the header) EXPOSE vs -p EXPOSE is a label; -p is the bridge RUN pip install Containers share nothing — install everything in the Dockerfile Layer caching requirements.txt first, code last — or every edit re-downloads deps TTL / max-age Always in seconds: 3600 = 1 hour, 7200 = 2 hours Cache-buster ?t=123 → new URL → cache miss → fresh fetch .env workflow .env + .gitignore + os.getenv() — never commit secrets 401 vs 403 Identity vs permission — no key vs wrong key 500 Server's problem — check backend + database, every layer crossed asyncio.gather Total = the max, not the sum. 4×1s + 1×10s = 10s Data leakage Test ≫ production = leakage. Memorization ≠ generalization Parquet Columnar binary — the "odd one out" vs text-based XML/JSON/CSV System > User LLMs weigh system prompts higher — the anti-injection defense Robust filter Lowercase + regex, never exact-string matching Structured Outputs Constrains generation (prevention). Python validation detects after RAG order Retrieve → Augment → Generate. Query is embedded before the LLM sees anything Chunk size 1–2 paragraphs (~200–500 words) — context vs focus Stale RAG docs Old chunks in the vector DB — the index, not the brain Race condition "Simultaneous" + "checks then writes" = both pass, both write Lookback + dedup Last ~3 days, keyed on (ID, timestamp) — never reprocess all history Serverless limits RAM (128–512 MB) + time (~10s edge) — long jobs go in containers Dependency pinning Reproducible = same install works tomorrow. Test upgrades separately

docs.title: 🟡 Traps — where marks are lost
docs.text: Trap The truth "CORS is a server error" It's a browser enforcement. curl/Postman are never blocked "Add the CORS header to the fetch call" Only the backend can grant permission "ls -h shows hidden files" -h = human-readable sizes. -a = all files "COUNT(col) = COUNT(*)" COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs "AVG includes NULLs as zero" NULLs are skipped: AVG of [10, 20, NULL] = 15 "High test accuracy = good model" Check for leakage first — memorized test rows inflate the score "GitHub Pages can host FastAPI" Static files only — no runtime, no database "I'll push the secret and remove it later" Git history is forever. Bots scan within minutes "More parallelism fixes slow requests" Gather = max, not sum. One hanger holds everything "Reprocess all history to catch late data" A failure of design — lookback + dedup instead

docs.title: 🔴 Wrong beliefs — commonly held, always wrong
docs.text: Wrong belief The reality "Structured Outputs guarantees accuracy" Only syntax — the model can still be wrong, grammatically "Fine-tuning makes the AI know your business" It changes behaviour, not facts. Prompt → RAG → tools → finetune, in that order "I can make the model immune to injection" You can only make a successful injection worthless — limit what it can do "Encryption means the data is safe at rest" HTTPS protects in transit; the endpoints still see plaintext "OpenRefine questions will be on the exam" Excluded this term — the professor said so explicitly "Old PYQs are the best prep" Only the recent era (T3-2025, T1-2026) matches current patterns

docs.title: The marks ramp — budget your time
docs.text:
Part 1 (1-mark, ~9 questions)  →  15 minutes max, move briskly
Part 2 (2-mark, ~5 questions)  →  15 minutes
Part 3 (3-mark, ~2 questions)  →  10 minutes
Part 4 (scenario blocks)       →  20 minutes — the big marks, don't rush
Part 5 (short answers)         →  15 minutes — structure matters

If you're running short: answer every remaining MCQ with your best guess (no negative marking), then write at least a structured skeleton for each short answer.

docs.title: Decision rules — the task → tool table
docs.text:
Task Tool Why Share results with a non-technical manager CSV Opens in Excel, zero friction Store large numeric arrays efficiently Parquet Columnar, 5–10× smaller, typed Expose a local app to the internet Tunnel (localtunnel/ngrok/Cloudflare) Public URL without deploying Deploy an ML demo HuggingFace Spaces Free, Gradio/Streamlit support Run a long batch job Container / VM No serverless time limits Handle a burst of short requests Serverless/edge Scales automatically, pay per use Catch late-arriving data in ETL Lookback + dedup Last N days, keyed on ID + timestamp Cache API responses TTL matching update frequency Bounded staleness, bounded load Secure an LLM from injection System/user roles + filtered input Role separation is primary, filtering is secondary Make an LLM return reliable JSON Structured Outputs Constrains generation, not just validates after

Official-topic must-remembers (new):

  • 🟢 p95/p99 beats the mean — the average hides the slow tail; latency targets are percentile targets
  • 🟢 Rates, not counts — "400 errors" means nothing without the denominator and window
  • 🟢 Liveness ≠ readiness — "process up" vs "can serve traffic"; readiness gates routing
  • 🟢 Idempotent writes — ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING / unique keys: a retry must be a no-op
  • 🟢 Staging + atomic swap — readers never see a half-loaded table
  • 🟢 Corrections keep provenance — old value, new value, reason, who, when — never destroy the record
  • 🟢 Untrusted triggers see no secrets — fork-PR CI runs with zero credentials
  • 🟢 A prompt is not a security boundary — authorization lives in code and retrieval scope, never in the system prompt
  • 🟢 Stateless servers, durable state — sessions in Redis/DB, work in queues; memory is disposable
  • 🟢 Identity vs delegated access — who you are vs what you're allowed on someone's behalf; tokens are scoped and revocable
  • 🟡 Deleted ≠ gone — a secret in history stays in every past commit; rotate first, then filter-repo + --force-with-lease
  • 🟡 Canary before full rollout — 5% of users for 2 minutes beats everyone for an hour; auto-rollback on error rates

docs.title: Data & ML — 60-second sheets
docs.text: ~7 min total · 6 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full: W6 + W8

docs.title: Parquet vs text formats
docs.text:
CSV/JSON/XML Parquet Structure Text-based, row-oriented Columnar binary Reading one column Parse every row Read only that column Size Baseline 5–10× smaller Types Everything is a string Real types preserved

The "odd one out" pattern

When XML, JSON, CSV are grouped in an efficiency question, Parquet (the columnar outlier) is the answer.

Practice: Why are Parquet queries faster than CSV on remote files?

Columnar storage — DuckDB downloads only the requested columns, not the whole file. → T1-AN Q4

docs.title: ML data leakage — the signature
docs.text:
Test accuracy wildly above production accuracy = leakage until proven otherwise.

Two ways it happens: 1. Temporal leakage: shuffling a chronological dataset — the model trains on tomorrow's patterns 2. Feature leakage: rolling stats computed before the train/test split — features contain future information

Wrong belief — '94% test accuracy means a good model'

If 200 test rows were in the training data, the model memorized them. After cleanup, the honest number appears (76% in the exam's example).

Practice: 99.2% test, 52% production. What caused the collapse?

Shuffling created temporal leakage; rolling stats before the split caused feature leakage. → T1-AN Q16

docs.title: Pandas — the exam's favourite operations
docs.text:
# Drop rows with missing text (for text analysis only)
df.dropna(subset=['review_text'])

# Filter + aggregate (the professor's exact line)
df.groupby('cuisine')['rating'].mean()

Trap — the NLP dropna

For text analysis, rows with no text are pure noise — drop them. But their ratings still count for non-text questions. Cleaning is per-question.

Practice: Average rating per cuisine — which operation?

df.groupby('cuisine')['rating'].mean() — split by cuisine, apply mean, combine. → T3-FN Q22

docs.title: ETL — the lookback + dedup pattern
docs.text:
The problem: late-arriving data that your daily pipeline already passed over.

The wrong fix: reprocess all history daily — "cost-extensive," a failure of design.

The right pattern: 1. Lookback window — process the last ~3 days, catching late arrivals 2. Deduplication — key on (order_id, update_timestamp); newest version wins

Practice: Orders from 2 days ago get updated. How do you catch them?

Lookback window + dedup on order ID and update timestamp. → T3-FN Q8

docs.title: Finetuning — when and when not
docs.text:
The escalation ladder (cheapest first)

1. Better prompting       → free, immediate
2. RAG (retrieval)        → model looks up facts
3. Tools/function calling → model delegates
4. Finetuning             → last resort, for stable repeated behaviour only

Good for: a fixed schema, a known format, a specialised vocabulary — stable, repeated behaviour.

NOT good for: changing facts, one-off tasks, unreliable workflows.

docs.title: Quantization — the trade-off
docs.text:
Precision Size Quality FP16 (baseline) — Full INT8 ~2× smaller Near-full INT4 ~4× smaller Noticeable loss

Smaller + faster + cheaper at the cost of some quality. The right level depends on the use case.

docs.title: Reading metrics — averages lie, percentiles don't
docs.text:
Official topic 1: Observability & Monitoring.

The mean hides the tail. 95 requests at 100ms + 5 at 5,000ms → mean ~345ms, which describes neither experience. Report:

  • p50 (median) — the typical experience
  • p95 — what your slow-but-normal users feel
  • p99 — the tail, where bugs live (a memory leak shows in p99 long before the mean moves)

Must remember — latency targets are percentile targets

"p95 under 500ms" is an SLO; "average under 500ms" is a wish. The mean is dominated by the bulk of requests — the slow tail that users complain about is invisible in it.

Trap — rates vs raw counts

"400 errors yesterday" is meaningless alone. 400/500 requests = catastrophe; 400/4M = noise. Always ask: count of what, over what denominator, in what window? A rising error count with flat traffic is an incident; with doubled traffic it's Tuesday.

Trap — averaging averages

Averaging per-day averages gives equal weight to a quiet Sunday and a Black Friday. Aggregate from raw events, or report percentiles per window.

docs.title: Health checks vs readiness — deployment's version of the same idea
docs.text:
Liveness Readiness Question is the process up? can I serve real traffic? Checks process responds at all DB connected, cache warm, dependencies up Failing it means restart me don't route users to me yet

Wrong belief — \"health check green = safe to receive traffic\"

A service can be alive with a dead DB connection — passing liveness, failing readiness. Readiness is the one that gates traffic. A load balancer watching only liveness keeps routing to a service that errors on every request.

docs.title: Cost tracking for AI systems
docs.text:
LLM features burn money per request — treat cost as a first-class metric: tokens in/out per request, cost per request, cost per successful request, daily spend vs budget. A runaway agent loop spends more in an afternoon than a month of normal traffic. Same alerting principles (rates, thresholds), applied to dollars.

→ Full treatment: Week 6 — reading metrics

docs.title: Data pipeline integrity — the five properties
docs.text:
Official topic 2: Data Pipeline Integrity.

A pipeline you can trust has five properties, each protecting the next:

1 · Stable identity + change detection. Every row needs an identity that survives re-reads (natural key, surrogate key, or content hash). "Changed" = the identity's payload differs from last time — not "I saw it again." A re-seen unchanged row is a no-op.

2 · Partial/failed run safety. The run died halfway — 60% written, 40% missing, dashboard already reading.

Must remember — staging + atomic swap

Write to a staging table and swap atomically when complete — readers never see a half-state. Alternatively, record run boundaries so downstream knows a load is partial. Never write row-by-row into the live table.

3 · Idempotency — safe retries. The write succeeded but the confirmation was lost; the retry doubles the row. Idempotent = same result run once or ten times: unique constraint on the natural key (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), dedup before write, or check-then-write against a processed-log.

Wrong belief — \"retries are rare, we'll handle them if they happen\"

Any pipeline that can be retried must be idempotent — retries always happen eventually. A webhook redelivery, a queue replay, a crash-restart: duplicates are normal input, not exceptions.

4 · Reproducibility. Same input + same code + same pinned dependencies = same output. Data: pinned snapshots, versioned queries, raw events retained. Models: fixed seeds, pinned libraries, experiment logs (parameters, metrics, artifacts). Without it, "the number changed" is undiagnosable.

5 · Provenance when correcting data. You fixed 300 rows. Six months later: which, why, who decided, what did they say before? Keep a correction log (row ID, old → new, reason, timestamp, who) or append-only versions.

Wrong belief — correcting data means overwriting it

Corrections never destroy the record of what was corrected. You may need to un-correct, or justify the correction to an auditor, later. The correction log (old value, new value, reason, who, when) is part of the correction.

Must remember — the chain in one line

identity → atomicity → idempotency → reproducibility → provenance. Each property protects the next.

→ Full treatment: Week 6 — pipeline integrity

docs.title: Docker & deployment — 60-second sheets
docs.text: ~7 min total · 6 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full treatment: W2

docs.title: Docker: EXPOSE vs -p
docs.text:
EXPOSE 8501        # documentation: "this app listens on 8501" — a LABEL

docker run -p 8501:8501 app   # THIS publishes the port to the host

The one-liner

EXPOSE is a label; -p is the bridge. If a container runs but localhost:8501 refuses to connect, you forgot -p.

Practice: Container runs, localhost:8501 doesn't connect. What's missing?

The -p 8501:8501 flag on docker run. → T1-AN Q28

docs.title: Docker: the missing install
docs.text:
A container that can't find the requests library is missing:

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

Containers are isolated — nothing from your laptop leaks in, including installed packages.

Practice: Why does the app work locally but crash in Docker?

The Dockerfile doesn't install dependencies. Containers share nothing with your laptop. → T1-FN Q11

docs.title: Docker: environment parity
docs.text:
An Ubuntu container built anywhere runs identically on Windows, macOS, Linux — the OS is inside the image. "Works on my machine" dies here.

Practice: You build on Linux, push to Docker Hub, colleague pulls on Windows. What happens?

It runs successfully. Docker packages the entire runtime environment. → T1-FN Q5

docs.title: Docker: layer caching
docs.text:
Docker rebuilds a layer only when its inputs change — and every layer after a changed layer rebuilds too.

COPY requirements.txt .              # ← dependency list FIRST
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt # ← install (stays cached)
COPY . .                            # ← code LAST

Trap — the build-speed killer

Copy the code before pip install and every code edit re-downloads every dependency. Copy requirements.txt first so the install layer stays cached.

Practice: Why does COPY . . before RUN pip install ruin builds?

Every code edit invalidates the COPY layer → the install layer after it rebuilds → dependencies re-download on every minor change. → T1-AN Q24 (short answer)

docs.title: Serverless limits — RAM + time as a pair
docs.text:
Limit The story The fix Time Edge function needs 40s, dies at 10s Long jobs → containers/queues RAM 2GB file works on laptop, dies on function (128–512 MB) Stream/chunk, don't load it all

The numbers

Your laptop: 8–32 GB RAM. Free-tier function: 128–512 MB. Edge timeout: ~10s.

Practice: A 2GB file crashes a serverless function but works locally. Why?

Free-tier functions enforce strict RAM limits (128–512 MB vs your laptop's 8–32 GB). → T1-FN Q10

docs.title: GitHub Pages — static only
docs.text:
Serves HTML, CSS, images, client-side JS. No server-side runtime, no database, no FastAPI backend. Form submissions have nothing to receive them.

Practice: Can you host a FastAPI backend on GitHub Pages?

No — Pages serves only static files. The backend needs a real runtime. → T1-FN Q3

docs.title: Git, security & practices — 60-second sheets
docs.text: ~6 min total · 5 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full: W1 + W7

docs.title: Git — the daily loop
docs.text:
Working dir --add--> Staging --commit--> Local repo --push--> GitHub
Command Shows git status Which files changed git diff What lines changed git log History git show One commit in detail

Trap — git diff after add shows nothing

git diff compares working dir to staging area. After git add, it's empty. Use git diff --staged.

Practice: Correct sequence to save and upload?

git add → git commit → git push. Always. → T3-FN Q23

docs.title: Merge conflicts + pull requests
docs.text:
Merge conflict: two people edit the same line on different branches. Git marks it (<<<<<<< / >>>>>>>), a human resolves it manually.

Pull request: a conversation about a merge — reviewers see the diff, comment, approve before merging.

Practice: Two people edit the same line. What happens on merge?

Git creates a merge conflict that must be resolved manually. → T3-FN Q24

docs.title: Secrets — the .env workflow
docs.text:
# .env (never committed)
API_KEY=sk-...

# .gitignore (add BEFORE first commit)
.env

# load in code
key = os.getenv("API_KEY")

Wrong belief — 'I'll push it now and remove it later'

Once pushed, the secret is in git history forever — clones, forks, scrapers. Bots scan for keys within minutes.

Practice: Which files go into .gitignore?

.env and any file containing secrets/credentials. Documentation and dependency lists do NOT. → T1-AN Q5

docs.title: Race conditions — the simultaneous write
docs.text:
Two users sign up with the same username at the same millisecond. Without locking: 1. Both availability checks pass simultaneously 2. Both writes proceed 3. Duplicate records or an exception

The fix: make check-and-write atomic — a database lock or a unique constraint.

Practice: What happens without locking on simultaneous signups?

Both checks pass, both create the user. → T1-FN Q16

docs.title: Dependency management — the middle path
docs.text:
Pin versions (pandas==2.2.0) for reproducibility. Test upgrades separately before applying. Never auto-upgrade everything or freeze forever.

The professional answer to every dependency question

  • Vulnerable old version + breaking new version? → Assess severity, test in staging, plan migration
  • New version with bug fixes? → Document current, test new separately, upgrade if compatible

Both extremes (immediately upgrade / never touch) are wrong in every paper.

Practice: Why pin dependencies?

Reproducible pipelines — prevents updates from breaking code. Same install works tomorrow. → T1-AN Q14

docs.title: Release security — what CI/CD must get right
docs.text:
Official topic 3: CI/CD & Release Security.

1 · Untrusted code never sees deploy credentials. Anyone can open a PR — so PR code is untrusted code. Tests on a fork PR run with zero secrets; deploy credentials only flow to trusted triggers (push/merge to main by maintainers).

Must remember — the trust of the trigger gates the secrets it sees

Fork-PR CI runs: tests execute, zero secrets are visible. Maintainer merges: deploy credentials may flow. The trust level of the event decides the privilege of the run.

Trap — the exfiltrating PR

A "test" that prints environment variables into the build log, or curls them to an external URL. If CI secrets were visible to PR runs, they're gone. Same defense as prompt injection: untrusted input never reaches privileged capabilities.

2 · Supply-chain hardening. Every dependency is attack surface you accepted:

  • Pin exact versions + lockfile — no latest, no loose flask>=2
  • Verify hashes — install what was reviewed, not what resolves today
  • Review dependency diffs in CI — not just your own code
  • Fewer dependencies — minimal surface

3 · Reviewing risky infra changes. A one-line Terraform change can open a database to the internet — infra blast radius is the whole system. Infra changes go through PR review with the plan/diff visible (what will this do?); anything touching security groups, credentials, or permissions gets a second, informed pair of eyes.

4 · Safe progressive rollouts. Deploy is a slope, not a switch:

canary (1-5%) -> staged (25% -> 50% -> 100%) -> full

Must remember — what a canary buys you

Each rollout step watches health rates (error rate, p95 — not raw counts) and auto-rolls-back on regression. A bad deploy then hurts 5% of users for two minutes, not everyone for an hour.

→ Full treatment: Week 7 — release security

docs.title: Safe git history changes — rewriting is surgery
docs.text:
Official topic 5: Web/API/Infra Fundamentals.

When history must change: a secret was committed, a giant file bloats the repo, garbage commits before going public.

The safe procedure:

  1. Rotate first if a secret was pushed — it was leaked the moment it left your machine; rewriting history does not un-leak it
  2. Rewrite on a branch, review, then:
git filter-repo --path .env --invert-paths
git push --force-with-lease        # not plain --force
  1. Coordinate — everyone rebases after the rewrite; announce it or spend a day untangling diverged histories

Must remember — force-with-lease over force

--force-with-lease refuses to overwrite if someone pushed in the meantime — history rewrites are the one place a plain force-push silently destroys teammates' work.

Trap — \"I deleted the file, so the secret is gone\"

Deleting the file in a new commit leaves it in every previous commit — still cloneable by anyone. Only rewrite + rotation fix it.

What rewriting costs

Every commit hash from the rewrite point back changes — tags, open PRs, and local clones reference dead IDs. Hence: rare, announced, surgical.

→ Full treatment: Week 2 — safe git history changes

docs.title: LLMs & prompting — 60-second sheets
docs.text: ~6 min total · 5 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full treatment: W3

docs.title: System vs user prompts
docs.text:
System prompt User prompt Carries Core rules, safety, identity The transient question Set by The developer The end user Weight Higher — the model obeys it more Lower

Why the hierarchy exists

LLMs assign higher attention weights to system prompts. A user typing "ignore previous instructions" can't easily override rules set in the system prompt — the model weighs system instructions more heavily by design.

Practice: Why separate core rules into a System prompt?

Models pay closer attention to System prompts, reducing user override attempts. → T1-FN Q15

docs.title: Structured Outputs
docs.text:
What it guarantees: valid JSON against your schema — token generation is constrained so invalid JSON cannot be produced.

What it does NOT guarantee: factual accuracy — the model can still be wrong, just grammatically correct.

The one-sentence difference from Python validation

Structured Outputs constrains generation (prevention — bad JSON can't happen). Python validation detects errors after (the model already produced bad JSON, your code catches it).

Practice: What's the key difference between Structured Outputs and Python validation?

Constrain generation vs detect after — prevention vs detection. → T1-FN Q22

docs.title: Prompt injection + the robust filter
docs.text:
The root cause: an LLM receives one flat stream of text — your system prompt and a hostile sentence arrive in the same channel. The model can't inherently tell instructions from data.

The defense layers (in order): 1. Role separation (system vs user) 2. Input normalization — lowercase + regex, not exact-string matching 3. Output validation (Pydantic schema) 4. Tool allow-listing (deny by default) 5. Human approval for destructive actions

Wrong belief — 'I'll just tell the model to ignore attacks'

You can't make a model immune by prompt alone. You CAN make a successful injection worthless by limiting what the system can do.

Practice: Blocking 'ignore' fails against 'IGNORE'. What's more robust?

Convert to lowercase + use regex for character substitutions. → T1-FN Q23

docs.title: OWASP LLM Top 10 — the vocabulary
docs.text:
Code Risk One-liner LLM01 Prompt Injection Untrusted text becomes instructions LLM02 Information Disclosure Model reveals secrets/PII LLM05 Improper Output Handling Output used unsanitised → XSS/SQLi LLM06 Excessive Agency Agent can do more than its task LLM07 System Prompt Leakage Your prompt becomes public LLM10 Unbounded Consumption Runaway tokens/cost

The audit question for your own project

LLM06: What is the worst single action my agent can take unsupervised? Most student projects fail this on first audit.

docs.title: Embeddings — the foundation for RAG
docs.text:
An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers representing the meaning of a text. Similar meanings → nearby vectors.

"King" − "Man" + "Woman" ≈ "Queen"

This powers semantic search, RAG, and recommendation systems — the query is embedded, matched against chunk embeddings, and the closest ones are retrieved.

Practice: What is an embedding?

A vector of numbers that encodes a text's meaning — the foundation of semantic search and RAG.

docs.title: Reliability discipline for LLM systems
docs.text:
Official topic 4: Reliable AI/LLM Systems.

1 · Verify AI output before trusting it. LLM output is evidence, not truth. The ladder, cheapest first:

  1. Schema validation — parses, has required fields (structured outputs give this by construction)
  2. Constraint checks in code — values in range, dates ordered, IDs exist. Your code checks; the LLM never self-certifies
  3. Grounding check — every factual claim traceable to a retrieved source
  4. Second-pass review — a separate model call or a human, before output acts or ships

Must remember — verification runs before the output is used

Not after problems appear: LLM drafts email → schema check → policy check → human approve → send. Skip a gate and the failure surfaces on the customer.

2 · Authorization in code, not prompts. "Never reveal internal documents" in a system prompt is a request; document permissions enforced in retrieval code is a control:

Defense Can it fail? Prompt instruction ("don't show X") yes — paraphrased injection slips past Retrieval scoping (X not in the corpus) no — nothing to leak Permission checks in code no — deterministic

Wrong belief — a system prompt is a security boundary

Sensitive-data boundaries live in architecture — what can be retrieved, what the code checks — never in what the model is asked not to do. A prompt is a request; code is a control.

3 · Structured output — see Structured Outputs. The phrase to remember: valid by construction, not by asking.

4 · Grounding in current sources — see the RAG staleness rules: expire old chunks, filter by effective date, no document → no answer.

→ Full treatment: Week 3 — reliability discipline

docs.title: RAG & agents — 60-second sheets
docs.text:
~7 min total · 6 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full: W4 + W5

New content this term — no PYQ history but GA-tested and expected on the exam.

docs.title: The RAG pipeline
docs.text:
Documents → Chunk → Embed → Vector DB
User query → Embed → Search → Retrieve top-K → Chunks + Query → LLM → Grounded answer

R = Retrieve → A = Augment → G = Generate. The query is embedded and matched against chunks before the LLM sees anything.

Practice: What happens FIRST in a RAG system?

Convert the query to an embedding and search for similar chunks — not generate, not store. R = first letter. → T3-AN Q34

docs.title: Chunking — the size trade-off
docs.text:
Size Problem Too small (1–2 sentences) Retrieved fragment lacks context to answer Too large (whole document) Embedding blurs + context window overflows Just right (1–2 paragraphs, ~200–500 words) Coherent enough to answer, focused enough to retrieve Practice: What chunk size for a customer support chatbot?

Medium chunks (~200–500 words) — context and focus balanced. → T3-AN Q36

docs.title: Stale documents — the RAG maintenance problem
docs.text:
The vector database is a snapshot. Ingest v1, ship v2, forget to remove v1's chunks — both embed, both retrieve, and the LLM can't tell which is authoritative.

The fix is operational: re-ingest atomically, version or timestamp chunks, expire the old.

Practice: Chatbot returns outdated manual info. Why?

Old chunks remain in the vector database — v1 wasn't removed when v2 was ingested. → T3-AN Q35

docs.title: asyncio.gather — the timing arithmetic
docs.text:
asyncio.gather launches all tasks simultaneously and returns only when every task completes.

The professor's arithmetic

5 requests: 4 take 1s, 1 takes 10s. Total: 10 seconds — the max, not the sum (14s sequential) or the average (5s). Concurrency removes the sum, not the max.

Practice: 4 requests at 1s + 1 at 60s in gather. What happens?

Waits 60s for all before returning. One hanger holds everything hostage. → T1-AN Q21

docs.title: Agents — the loop and the guardrails
docs.text:
An agent = a model that chooses and uses tools repeatedly to finish a goal.

Goal → Decide → Use a tool → Observe → (repeat) → Done

The parts that matter: - Tools — what the agent can do (allow-list, deny by default) - Rules — limits on steps, time, cost - Verifier — checks whether the result is correct

Trap — LLM06 Excessive Agency

What's the worst single action your agent can take unsupervised? If the answer is "send_email" or "delete" without human approval, that's the vulnerability.

docs.title: MCP — Model Context Protocol
docs.text:
A standard protocol for connecting LLMs to external tools and data sources — the "USB-C of AI integrations." Instead of custom integrations per tool, MCP provides a common interface.

Sandboxing — running agent actions in isolated environments (containers, VMs, LXC) so a compromised agent can't damage your host or exfiltrate data.

docs.title: Web & APIs — 60-second sheets
docs.text: ~6 min total · 5 concepts · Last-minute revision layer — full treatment: W2

docs.title: CORS — Same-Origin Policy
docs.text:
Origin = scheme + host + port. Different ports = different origins, even on localhost.

The browser blocks JavaScript on one origin from reading a response from another — unless the receiving server explicitly allows it via Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

Why it exists

Web apps load nested third-party JavaScript. If compromised, it could silently exfiltrate your data to evil.com. The policy is the guardrail; CORS is the gate.

Practice: Frontend on :3000, backend on :8000 — who fixes the CORS error?

The backend, by adding the allowed origin to its response headers. The frontend can't grant itself permission. → T1-AN Q13

docs.title: HTTP status codes — the family
docs.text:
Code Meaning Action 200 OK — 401 Unauthorized — who are you? Check your API key 403 Forbidden — you can't do this Check permissions 404 Not found Check the URL 429 Rate limit — slow down Wait, retry with backoff 500 Server error — their problem Check backend + database

Trap — 401 vs 403

Identity vs permission. A locked door with no key (401) vs a key that doesn't fit this lock (403).

Practice: A 500 error in a scenario — where do you look?

Backend code and database layers — not the frontend. Every layer the request crossed is suspect. → T1-FN Q28

docs.title: Caching — TTL, Cache-Control, cache-buster
docs.text:
Concept What it does TTL How long a cached copy is fresh — always in seconds (3600 = 1 hour) Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 Authorizes proxies + CDNs to serve copies Cache-buster (?t=123) A new URL = cache miss = fresh fetch from origin

Trap — the units ladder

"max-age=7200 — how long?" → 2 hours. Not milliseconds, not minutes, not days. Seconds, always.

Practice: How do you force fresh data past a cache?

Append a random query parameter (?t=123) — the URL changes, so the cache key changes, so it's a miss. → T1-AN Q22

docs.title: API gateway — the single entry point
docs.text:
What it is: one URL that routes to many backend services, with centralized authentication.

Why: 80 hardcoded URLs in a mobile app break during migrations; 80 separate auth implementations are inconsistent.

The failure: a single gateway = single point of failure. During a traffic spike, it crashes and takes the platform down.

The fix: multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer.

Practice: A 500 behind a gateway — what do you check?

Every layer: routing logic, auth middleware, the service itself, and the network between them. → T1-FN Q28

docs.title: HTTPS — why encryption matters
docs.text:
HTTP sends data in cleartext — anyone intercepting reads your token. HTTPS encrypts it end-to-end.

The professor's model: the Caesar cipher (shift every letter by 2) — a toy algorithm that perfectly explains the principle: scramble in transit, unscramble at the ends.

Practice: Why is HTTPS recommended for API tokens?

Tokens over HTTP are readable by anyone on the network path. HTTPS encrypts them so only sender and receiver can read. → T1-FN Q6

docs.title: Statelessness & durable storage — why servers are allowed to die
docs.text:
Official topic 5: Web/API/Infra Fundamentals.

Stateless = the server remembers nothing between requests. Any request can hit any instance; any instance can be killed and replaced. That's what makes scaling and deploys safe.

State lives elsewhere — durably:

State Lives in Must survive database Fast lookups Redis / cache Work for later queue → worker Who you are between requests session store / token

Trap — the in-memory login dict

Works locally, works with one instance; the platform restarts the container (serverless does this constantly) and everyone's logged out — or a second instance means half your users "don't exist." Sessions belong in Redis/DB; in-memory caches are disposable (rebuildable) state.

Must remember — the pattern that follows

Stateless API → durable queue → worker → database. Each part crashes, restarts, and scales independently — it's the serverless-limits workaround and the resilience story, unified.

→ Full treatment: Week 2 — statelessness

docs.title: API error design — failing usefully
docs.text:
Official topic 5: Web/API/Infra Fundamentals.

The code carries the category, the body carries the diagnosis:

Code Meaning Who fixes it 400 malformed request caller 401 not authenticated — who are you? caller (credentials) 403 authenticated, not permitted caller (permissions) 404 doesn't exist (or hidden on purpose) caller's URL 422 well-formed, semantically invalid (Pydantic) caller's data 429 rate limit — slow down caller, eventually 500 our code/dependencies failed server team

Must remember — a useful error names the specifics

Field, problem, ideally the fix: {"error": "quantity must be >= 1, got 0", "field": "quantity"} — not a bare 400. Fail fast, fail loud: reject bad input at the boundary before processing; silent acceptance is the 3am scenario where the error surfaces far from its cause.

Never leak internals

Stack traces to the client map your code (a security hole). Log the trace server-side; return a clean message + a request ID the user can quote.

CORS / authN / authZ are three different problems

CORS = the browser's cross-origin read rule (fixed by the server's response headers). Authentication = identity (401). Authorization = permission (403). Each failure is fixed by a different party — exams mix them deliberately.
